label: Candidate: Lead Data Platform Engineer
jd: Lead Data Platform Engineer: design large-scale Apache Spark and Iceberg lakehouse architectures, optimize table partitioning and streaming ingestion, ensure data reliability, and collaborate with analytics and product teams on schema evolution. 5+ years of experience.
resume:
Meera Kulkarni | meera.k@example.com | +91 97654 32109
Lead Data Platform Engineer, 7 years
- Designed and deployed an Apache Iceberg lakehouse on AWS EMR processing 18 TB/day with sub-second query pruning
- Optimized Spark streaming ingestion pipelines, slashing compute costs by 45% using z-order clustering and compaction
- Built automated data quality validation frameworks using Great Expectations
- Drove company-wide data governance and schema evolution across analytics teams
Skills: Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg, Scala, Python, AWS EMR, Presto/Trino, Kafka
transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome, Meera. Walk me through how you optimized the Iceberg lakehouse for 18 TB daily volume.
Candidate: Our raw streaming events arrived via Kafka and were written to S3 via Spark Structured Streaming with 1-minute microbatches. Queries were scanning hundreds of thousands of small files. I implemented automated Iceberg compaction jobs running every four hours, sorted the tables with Z-Order clustering on customer_id and event_timestamp, and enabled Bloom filters on high-cardinality keys. Read query latency dropped by 75% and S3 compute costs fell by 45%.
Interviewer: How do you handle schema evolution across downstream analytics teams?
Candidate: Iceberg supports full in-place schema evolution with column ID tracking, so column renames and additions don't break existing data. When downstream BI queries failed due to type mismatches, I added schema enforcement gates in Great Expectations that reject malformed producer events before they enter the silver layer.
Interviewer: How do you work with data analysts and business stakeholders when schema changes occur?
Candidate: To be candid, data analysts constantly complain when columns change, but I expect them to adapt their SQL queries. I don't give advance deprecation warnings because that delays engineering sprints. If their dashboards break, they can inspect our schema registry.
Interviewer: Have you had disagreements with product or data science leads?
Candidate: Yes, the data science lead wanted uncurated raw access to our production metastore. I refused and blocked their IAM permissions without discussion. They escalated to the VP of Engineering, but I don't compromise on architecture boundaries, even if it creates friction with teams.
